title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service recorded work meetings by default and used the recordings to train its AI system without securing explicit consent from all meeting participants. The system was deployed to collect data at scale, processing over one billion meetings, with the company relying on host-level permissions rather than requiring individual participant consent. This deployment failed to implement a control that would have been straightforward: obtaining affirmative agreement from every person whose voice would be recorded and whose words would be fed into a machine learning pipeline.

The company's approach to consent appears to have been a checkbox process that the lawsuit contests as ineffective, and the system sometimes joined meetings automatically through calendar integrations without alerting participants to the recording. It is not established whether the recordings were adequately anonymized before training, whether Otter's consent disclosures were sufficient under the law, or whether the company intended to circumvent participant notification.

summary:
# Summary

A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View technology company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission and using them to train its artificial intelligence transcription service. The suit, brought by plaintiff Justin Brewer, claims the company's Otter Notebook tool, used for real-time transcriptions of virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams, violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws. The company records meetings by default without alerting all participants that their conversations will be shared with Otter for AI improvement purposes. Approximately 25 million people currently use Otter's transcription tools, which have processed over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016.

The lawsuit challenges Otter's claim that it obtains explicit permission through user checkboxes and questions the effectiveness of the company's process for anonymizing recorded data before using it for machine learning. Multiple users have reported problems on social media platforms, including instances where Otter automatically joined meetings through integrated workplace calendars and recorded conversations without consent. The company maintains it receives proper authorization, though it does not require all meeting participants to grant permission individually when a meeting host has an active Otter account.
